news_drafts.headline: Waltham Forest holds £543.6m of borrowing, with £131.5m of it due within 12 months
news_drafts.lead:
Waltham Forest Council owed £543.6m in loans at 30 September 2026, at an average interest rate of 3.93% and with an average of 18.6 years until they fall due. The figures are in the mid-year treasury management report (the council's account of how it borrows and invests spare cash) for full council on 22 October. Of the total, £449.5m, or 82.7%, is from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB), the government's lending arm for councils. Another £61.0m is in temporary loans.

The report's maturity profile, which sets out when loans fall due, puts 24.19% of the borrowing, about £131.5m, for repayment within 12 months. The council's approved range for loans falling due in that period is 0% to 75%. Loans that fall due can be paid off or refinanced, meaning a new loan is taken to repay the old one.

The report also says the council did not take out any long-term PWLB loans in the six months to 30 September 2026.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix - 2026-27 Treasury Managment Strategy Mid- Year Report (Full Council)

news_drafts.headline: Waltham Forest forecasts spending its own cash in place of loans to fall from £100.2m to £64.6m by 2030/31
news_drafts.lead:
Waltham Forest Council expects the amount of its capital spending paid for from its own cash, rather than from loans, to fall from £100.236m in 2026/27 to £64.587m by 2030/31, a drop of about 35%. The forecast is in the council's mid-year treasury management report (how a council borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both), which goes to the Audit and Governance Committee on 14 October.

The report calls this under-borrowing, or internal borrowing: using the council's own cash reserves instead of taking a loan, which saves interest but uses up the cushion. It is the gap between the council's capital financing requirement (the total it has spent on long-lived assets that it has not yet paid for, in effect its underlying need to borrow) and the borrowing it actually holds. The forecast runs from £92.557m in 2027/28 to £83.923m in 2028/29 and £74.312m in 2029/30. The paper attributes the fall to a growing capital financing requirement while the capital programme, the council's planned spending on things that last, remains elevated.

For 2025-26, the council's statement of accounts, its formal annual accounts, put the position at £155m. That is a capital financing requirement of £777m, less £545m of borrowing, £26m under private finance initiative contracts and £51m of lease liabilities.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix - 2026-27 Treasury Managment Strategy Mid- Year Report v.1

news_drafts.headline: Waltham Forest forecasts £6.4m exceptional financial support for 2026/27, down from £19m agreed
news_drafts.lead:
Waltham Forest Council now expects to need £6.4m of exceptional financial support (EFS) in 2026/27, against the £19m agreed in principle in its February 2026 budget. EFS is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort. The figure, a 66% reduction, comes from a medium-term financial strategy report (the council's plan for the next few years) going to Cabinet on 6 October.

The report bases the £6.4m on the month 3 budget monitoring, the in-year check of spending against budget. It gives three reasons for the fall: £3.8m of additional funding from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, £5.7m of new savings identified during the year, and net underspends in corporate balances.

The council remains dependent on EFS borrowing to balance the year, though at a much lower level than first anticipated. The paper says the forecast "is subject to new pressures emerging by year end."
news_drafts.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 27 - Cabinet report

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Pension Fund Annual Report 25-26 - Draft
findings.headline: Fund committed to London CIV Nature Based Solutions and Private Debt II funds and transferred funds to them during the year
findings.detail: The paper lists the year's investment strategy steps: divestment from the LCIV Global Equity Focus Fund and the LCIV Passive Equity Progressive Paris Aligned Fund, new investment in the LCIV MAC Fund and the Short Duration Buy and Maintain Credit Fund, and commitments to two new LCIV funds. It also notes further transfers into the Renewable Infrastructure and Global Infrastructure Partners funds.
findings.matters: Commitments to private market and infrastructure funds are long-dated and drawn down over time, so they tie up cash that a finance director would otherwise see as liquid.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Pension Fund Annual Report 25-26 - Draft
findings.headline: Net assets of the Fund rose £77.6m, from £1,091.5m at 31 March 2025 to £1,169.1m at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to net contributions of £5m, investment income net of expenses of £16.3m, and a net gain on investments of £1.1m. These components sum to £22.4m, so the paper's narrative does not reconcile fully to the £77.6m increase, which it does not explain.
findings.matters: A reader comparing the Fund's asset growth with its reported drivers would need the reconciling item, which the paper does not provide.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Pension Fund Annual Report 25-26 - Draft
findings.headline: Forecast cash surplus carried forward rises from £16.8m at 31 March 2026 to £27.5m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The three-year cashflow forecast shows net cash inflows in each forecast year, with pension payments and expenses exceeding contributions and transfers. Balances are shown in brackets as surpluses in the paper's table.
findings.matters: A cash surplus that grows through the forecast period means the Fund does not need to sell assets to pay benefits, a point lenders and finance directors read as liquidity.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Pension Fund Annual Report 25-26 - Draft
findings.headline: Mercer's rebalancing review found the Fund overweight in equities held in London CIV
findings.detail: The paper says the rebalancing was carried out ahead of the 2025 valuation to test whether changes to the strategic allocation would affect employer contributions. It reports the Fund intends to reduce exposure to high-variability growth assets.
findings.matters: A finance officer at another council in the London CIV pool would want to know whether their own pooled equity exposure has the same risk finding.
findings.quote: The outcome of the rebalancing performed by Mercers highlighted that the Fund was overweight in equities held in London CIV.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Pension Fund Annual Report 25-26 - Draft
findings.headline: Current equity weighting of 52.5% is above the 40.0-50.0% allowable range in the Fund's benchmark table
findings.detail: The paper's Table 1 compares current weightings with the strategic benchmark and the allowable ranges. Fixed income is at 23.9% against a 27.5-37.5% range, and alternatives at 17.1% against 15.0-30.0%. The paper says the Fund will move away from growth assets to alternatives as per the strategic allocation.
findings.matters: A fund outside its own allowable ranges is a governance point an auditor or pensions regulator would review, and it shows how far the portfolio sits from its target mix.
